entities.name: An-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qaitbay
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
An-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qaitbay, who reigned from August 7, 1496, until his assassination on October 31, 1498, was a Mamluk sultan of Egypt whose brief and tumultuous tenure epitomized the accelerating internal decay of the late Burji Mamluk Sultanate. As the designated heir to his long-reigning and powerful father, Sultan Qaitbay, An-Nasir Muhammad's inability to consolidate authority quickly exposed the severe factionalism, military rivalries, and succession crises that were fundamentally undermining the Mamluk state's stability and strength on the cusp of significant Ottoman expansion into the Levant.

Elevated to the throne at a young age, An-Nasir Muhammad inherited a sultanate grappling with profound internal challenges and increasing external pressures. His reign was immediately defined by intense power struggles among the senior Mamluk emirs, who fiercely competed for control over the inexperienced sultan and the reins of government. He functioned largely as a figurehead, manipulated by powerful factions, most notably those led by the ambitious Khushqadam and later Tumanbay. These rivalries manifested in frequent coups and counter-coups, severely eroding central authority and precipitating widespread unrest within Cairo and across the Mamluk provinces, including Syria. Despite his nominal position, An-Nasir Muhammad struggled to assert personal rule, instead becoming a pawn in the shifting alliances of Mamluk commanders.
